lead: IoT analytics turns a flood of sensor readings into summaries, alerts and models. A vibration sensor may send 2,000 samples every second, far too much for a person to read. Analytics filters and aggregates at the edge, stores recent values for live dashboards, keeps raw data for later batch training, and raises an alert when a motor starts to fail. It exists because bandwidth, storage and human attention are limited. It is used in factories, smart grids, vehicle fleets and city water systems.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 sensor sampling; Chapter 5.2 platform routing; basic DBMS.

sections.h3: Streams, batches and the four Vs

blocks.text: IoT data arrives as a stream: an ordered flow of readings, each with a time stamp. Stream processing handles each reading as it arrives and answers in seconds. Batch processing stores readings first and processes them later in large groups. A motor monitor uses both: a stream job raises a high-vibration alert now, while a nightly batch job retrains a failure model on a month of history.

Four properties describe the load. Volume is the total amount, for example 28.8 MB per hour from one vibration sensor. Velocity is the arrival rate, here 2,000 samples per second. Variety is the mix of types: numbers, status codes, images and logs. Veracity is how far the data can be trusted, since a loose wire can send zeros that look valid.

Edge pre-processing cuts the stream before it reaches the cloud. Filtering drops known-bad values. Windowing groups readings by time, such as 1-minute tumbling windows that do not overlap. Aggregation replaces a window with one summary: average, minimum, maximum or count.

blocks.where: x̄ is the window average; x<sub>i</sub> are the sample values inside the window; n is the number of samples in the window.

items: Open a window of fixed length, such as 60 s.
Apply a filter, for example keep only values from 0 to 50 mm/s.
Compute one aggregate for the window.
Send the aggregate and its time stamp to the cloud.

blocks.text: A time-series store is a database built for timestamped values. It indexes by time and by sensor id, so a query for the last hour of one motor is fast. Many designs keep two layers. A hot store holds recent values for dashboards and usually keeps days or weeks. A raw store keeps every sample, or a compressed form, for audits and model training.

Big data tools split work across machines. Hadoop HDFS stores large files in blocks spread over many disks, with copies for fault tolerance. MapReduce is a batch model: a map step transforms records, then a reduce step combines them by key. Spark runs batch and stream jobs and keeps working data in memory, which helps iterative training. A Kafka-style log ingests many device streams in order and lets several consumers read the same data. NoSQL stores, such as key-value or document databases, hold device metadata and flexible JSON records.

blocks.text: Visualization turns tables into decisions. A line plot shows a trend over time. A gauge shows the current value against a safe range. A heat map shows many sensors at once. A dashboard combines these views with a time range selector. The dashboard reads the hot store, so it must show data freshness, such as 'last update 12 s ago'.

An alert is a rule or model that fires when action is needed. A simple threshold alert fires when vibration exceeds 45 mm/s for 3 minutes. A smarter alert compares the current window with a learned baseline. Alerts must avoid fatigue: too many false alarms and operators ignore them.

In Industry 4.0, predictive maintenance uses vibration, temperature and current sensors on motors and pumps. A model learns normal behaviour and estimates remaining useful life. Maintenance is scheduled before failure, not after a breakdown. A simple sensor node does three jobs: sense, process a window locally, and send a summary with its device id.

examples.question: A vibration sensor samples 2,000 times per second, 4 bytes per sample. Find raw data per hour. If the edge keeps only a one-minute average (one value per minute) for the dashboard, find the reduction factor in stored values per hour.
steps: Samples per hour = 2,000 samples/s × 3,600 s/h = 7,200,000 samples/h.
Raw bytes per hour = 7,200,000 samples/h × 4 bytes/sample = 28,800,000 bytes/h.
Dashboard values per hour = 60 min/h × 1 value/min = 60 values/h.
Reduction factor = 7,200,000 raw samples/h ÷ 60 dashboard values/h = 120,000.
examples.answer: Raw data is 7,200,000 samples/h, 28,800,000 bytes/h or 28.8 MB/h; the dashboard stores 60 values/h, a reduction factor of 120,000 times.
examples.check:
samples_per_second = 2000
bytes_per_sample = 4
seconds_per_hour = 3600
samples_per_hour = samples_per_second * seconds_per_hour
bytes_per_hour = samples_per_hour * bytes_per_sample
mb_per_hour = bytes_per_hour / 1_000_000
dashboard_values_per_hour = 60
reduction = samples_per_hour / dashboard_values_per_hour
print(samples_per_hour)
print(bytes_per_hour)
print(mb_per_hour)
print(dashboard_values_per_hour)
print(reduction)

traps: Sampling rate is samples per second, not bytes per second. Multiply by bytes per sample before quoting MB.
A one-minute average stores 60 values per hour, not 60 samples per second. Do not multiply by 60 again.
Stream processing answers in seconds; batch processing runs later on stored data. A dashboard fed by a daily batch is not live.
Variety and veracity are different: variety is different data types, veracity is trustworthiness.
A dashboard is a view, not the database. Closing the dashboard does not delete the raw store.

quiz.q: Define velocity and variety for IoT data.
quiz.a: Velocity is the rate at which readings arrive, such as 2,000 samples/s. Variety is the mix of data types, such as numeric readings, status codes and images.

quiz.q: Why does edge pre-processing lower cloud cost?
quiz.a: It sends one summary per window instead of every sample, so less bandwidth and fewer stored records; it also drops bad values early. The worked example reduces 7,200,000 raw samples/h to 60 dashboard values/h.

quiz.q: A sensor sends 500 samples/s, 2 bytes each. Find raw MB per hour and the reduction if the edge stores one value per 30 s.
A live dashboard is flat but threshold alerts keep firing. Give two plausible causes and one check for each.
quiz.a: The dashboard may read a stale hot-store cache while alerts read the raw stream; check last-update time. The dashboard may plot a 1-hour average while alerts use 1-minute windows; check the window length. Or the dashboard may filter out the faulty sensor id; check the query filter.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a hot store and a raw store?
quiz.a: A hot store keeps recent values for fast dashboard queries and usually keeps days or weeks. A raw store keeps every sample, or a compressed form, for audits and model training.

quiz.q: A 1-minute window holds values 10, 12, 14, 16 mm/s. Compute the window average.
Why train a predictive-maintenance model daily in batch rather than retrain on every reading?
quiz.a: Training on every reading is expensive and unstable; daily batch uses enough history, keeps the model reproducible, and the live stream only applies the model. Retraining can wait unless drift is detected.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern IoT analytics often uses a lakehouse: cheap object storage for raw data plus a table layer for SQL queries. Stream SQL and complex event processing let analysts write window queries without custom code. Time-series compression, such as delta-of-delta encoding, cuts storage for slowly changing signals. Federated learning trains models across gateways without sending every raw sample to the cloud. Search for 'time-series database', 'Kafka stream processing' and 'predictive maintenance feature engineering' to go deeper.
